name: Septoria leaf spot complex
summary: A plant-linked Cannabis leaf-spot complex in which lower- or inner-canopy onset, expanding brown lesions with yellow halos, and pycnidia are compatible evidence. Images can support a Septoria differential but cannot resolve the pathogen: S. cannabicola is a distinct seven-locus lineage from the Kentucky isolates labeled S. cannabis, whose original species assignment lacked an ex-type sequence comparison.
affectedParts: whole canopy for distribution and defoliation context
culture, voucher, and sequence records linked to the sampled lesion
indicators: Compatible symptoms begin primarily on older lower leaves or in the inner canopy, but canopy position varies with cultivar, site, season, crop architecture, and competing leaf-spot diseases.

Early lesions may be indistinct yellow or small irregular brown-to-gray spots and can develop brown circular-to-irregular centers with yellow halos; none of these colors or shapes is unique to Septoria.

Kentucky S. cannabis-associated lesions expanded rapidly to about 5 to 7.5 mm, while Japanese S. cannabicola lesions were described as about 2 to 8 mm; these overlapping study ranges are descriptive rather than diagnostic thresholds.

Mature lesions may contain scattered round brown-to-black pycnidia visible with magnification and sometimes to the unaided eye; verify that dots are embedded fungal structures rather than debris, frass, or unrelated growth.
Under moist conditions, pycnidia may exude thin white curled or ribbon-like conidial tendrils, a useful Septoria-complex sign that still does not determine species from a photograph.
Repeated observations can show increasing lesion number, expansion, coalescing halos, yellowing, canopy loss, and premature defoliation of older leaves.
Lesion-linked culture and compatible pycnidia and conidia strengthen an organism label; conidial septation, dimensions, and morphology require calibrated laboratory observation.
Species-level evidence requires traceable isolates, morphology, vouchers, and validated multilocus comparison: the Japanese ex-type and Kentucky isolates occupy different phylogenetic clades.
exclusions: Sooty or olivaceous reproductive growth concentrated on the lower leaf surface plus lesion-linked Pseudocercospora evidence supports olive or sooty leaf spot rather than Septoria.
Pale-centered round lesions with melanized conidiophores and a lesion-linked Cercospora identification support Cercospora leaf spot.
Concentric rings or dark central sporulation plus lesion-linked Alternaria evidence support Alternaria, although rings and dark centers alone remain nonspecific.
Compatible Bipolaris conidia or culture and validated lesion-linked molecular evidence support Bipolaris; canopy position and lesion color cannot separate the two diseases.
Acervuli, setae, compatible conidia, or molecular evidence from the lesion support Colletotrichum anthracnose rather than a Septoria label.
Angular water-soaked lesions, bacterial streaming or ooze, and a lesion-linked bacterial isolate support bacterial leaf spot.
Punctures, stippling, mines, chewing, frass, webbing, larvae, mites, or thrips explain the pattern and exclude a symptom-only Septoria label.
A sharp spray, row, field-edge, lighting, irrigation, abrasion, or contact boundary without compatible organism evidence supports chemical, environmental, or mechanical injury.
A symmetric leaf-age or canopy pattern with matched pH, EC, moisture, root, or tissue evidence supports a nutrient or root-zone disorder rather than confirmed Septoria.
A different dominant lesion-linked organism, mixed recovery without causal resolution, or symptomless appropriate inoculation controls excludes a confirmed single-pathogen Septoria label.

progression.description: Record plant ID, cultivar, planting date, canopy levels, field or room position, recent wetness, irrigation, airflow, residue, treatments, and matched symptom-free plants before assigning a pathogen.
Tag intact lower- or inner-canopy leaves with indistinct yellow or small brown-gray spots and photograph the whole plant, whole leaf, both surfaces, and calibrated lesion macro views.
Reimage the same leaves as lesions enlarge, become brown and circular-to-irregular, develop halos, or produce visible pycnidia; preserve advancing margins before treatment.
Document pycnidia, any moist-condition conidial tendrils, lesion coalescence, yellowing, and defoliation while retaining plant and lesion linkage.

Link culture, microscopy, pathogenicity, voucher, loci, sequences, and phylogenetic interpretation to the photographed lesion; retain a complex-level label unless the evidence supports a named species.

lookAlikes: Pseudocercospora olive or sooty leaf spot
Stemphylium or other fungal leaf spot
Caterpillar, beetle, slug, or snail feeding
Hail, wind, handling, abrasion, or training injury
Nutrient, pH, salinity, drought, or root-zone stress
confirmation: Capture a traceable series from the same plant: whole canopy, upper/middle/lower canopy, both leaf surfaces, lesion-center and advancing-margin macros with a scale, and matched unaffected tissue.

Record plant ID, cultivar, stage, propagation source, onset date, field or room map, canopy position, recent rain or irrigation, humidity and leaf wetness when available, airflow, residue, and spray or mechanical exposures.
Use a hand lens or microscope to verify embedded pycnidia and any conidial tendrils; black dots, lesion size, yellow halos, or lower-canopy position alone cannot confirm Septoria.

Before treatment, submit fresh tissue spanning healthy and advancing lesion margins to a qualified plant diagnostic laboratory and preserve chain of custody between the plant, image, specimen, culture, and result.
For a Septoria-complex organism label, use compatible lesion-linked culture, pycnidial and conidial morphology, and validated molecular evidence while retaining mixed-organism findings.

For S. cannabis, S. cannabicola, or another species label, preserve isolate and voucher identifiers and require an appropriate multilocus comparison; generic PCR, ITS-only, single-locus, morphology-only, and image-only evidence remain provisional.

When causality matters, require compatible symptom reproduction, recovery of the same organism, and symptomless appropriate controls; do not universalize the Japanese study's unexpected absence of symptoms on wounded inoculated leaves.

Keep symptom-only, detached-leaf-only, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, generic-PCR, ITS-only, single-locus, low-resolution, generated, vendor, anecdotal, forum, and unverified samples out of the confirmed class and route them to human review.
immediateActions: Preserve representative untreated tissue and traceable photographs before pruning or applying a product.
Separate symptomatic propagation material from clean stock and reduce avoidable prolonged leaf wetness while diagnosis is pending.
Map affected plants by cultivar, canopy level, irrigation or wetness zone, airflow, residue, field edge, and possible abiotic boundaries.
correctivePlan: Use sanitation, environmental management, and any treatment only after the causal organism and production context are sufficiently resolved.
Remove or contain confirmed diseased leaves and fallen residue as locally appropriate, then monitor tagged plants for new lesion incidence and severity.
Treat the 2023-2024 TJ's CBD field results as one isolate-cultivar-location evidence set; verify current local pesticide registration and label requirements before any application.
prevention: Use clean propagation material and avoid moving symptomatic plants, tools, or debris into clean areas.
Improve air circulation, reduce avoidable humidity and leaf wetness, and manage infected foliage or residue where feasible.
Scout consistent plant IDs across canopy levels and over time so early lesions, pycnidia development, and confounders can be separated.
warnings: Image or video alone is capped at 0.25 confidence because lower-canopy brown lesions, yellow halos, pycnidia-like dots, and defoliation overlap other fungal, bacterial, arthropod, and abiotic injuries.
The label is a Septoria leaf-spot complex unless lesion-linked laboratory evidence resolves the organism; a photograph cannot distinguish S. cannabis from S. cannabicola.

The 2021 Kentucky S. cannabis assignment used morphology and seven loci but lacked published S. cannabis reference sequences; the 2024 Japanese ex-type S. cannabicola occupies a different clade, and historical ex-type sequences remain unavailable.

Lesion dimensions, conidial measurements, canopy distribution, inoculation response, timing, cultivar effects, disease progress, and product efficacy are bounded to the cited studies and are not universal thresholds.

The hemp disease cycle remains incompletely established; debris survival, stomatal entry, wind or water dispersal, and polycyclic spread should be recorded as plausible epidemiology rather than certain reconstruction of an individual case.

No media was added: the Japanese article presents conflicting license statements and a mixed natural-symptom, inoculation, microscopy, and culture figure, while the Cornell photographs lack item-level reuse terms.
Pesticide efficacy does not confirm diagnosis, and every application must follow current product labeling, registration, resistance-management, worker-safety, and jurisdictional requirements.
Human review remains mandatory for symptom-only, detached, mixed-pathogen, culture-unlinked, generic-PCR, ITS-only, single-locus, species-inferred, low-resolution, or rights-unclear samples.

sources.title: Reemergence of Septoria Leaf Spot Caused by Septoria cannabis on Hemp in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Kentucky hemp symptoms occurred mostly on lower leaves and in the inner canopy; small irregular brown-to-gray spots rapidly expanded to about 5 to 7.5 mm and contained scattered round dark-brown-to-black pycnidia.

The reported pycnidia measured 38.8 to 145 micrometres, and conidia were hyaline, curved or occasionally straight, pointed at the apex, and three- to four-septate; these laboratory signs are stronger than lesion color alone but are not camera-level species proof.
Eight isolates were tested for pathogenicity on six-week-old greenhouse hemp, and three isolates were sequenced at seven loci: elongation factor, beta-tubulin, RPB2, LSU, ITS, actin, and calmodulin.

No published Septoria accessions matched the seven-locus sequences and no S. cannabis reference sequences were then available; the Kentucky S. cannabis conclusion combined morphology, phylogenetic separation from other Septoria species, and the absence of a better sequence match.

The study sampled several Kentucky locations in 2018 and tested two greenhouse hemp cultivars; its lesion sizes, timing, canopy distribution, and taxonomy are not universal thresholds for every Cannabis crop or Septoria lineage.
Visual lesion appearance alone cannot separate Septoria from other hemp leaf-spot pathogens or distinguish S. cannabis from S. cannabicola.

sources.title: Septoria cannabicola, a new species on Cannabis sativa from Japan
supportedClaims: A 2023 commercial-hemp sample from Mie Prefecture, Japan yielded the ex-type isolate MUCC3619 and voucher TSU-MUMH11996; morphology and a seven-locus phylogeny established the distinct species Septoria cannabicola.

Natural symptoms began as indistinct angular yellow spots on lower leaves, developed into brown circular-to-irregular lesions with yellow halos measuring about 2 to 8 mm, and caused premature defoliation of older leaves.

At 14 days after inoculation, intact inoculated leaves developed field-like symptoms while water controls and, unexpectedly, wounded inoculated leaves did not; that single experimental result must not be converted into a universal wound-response rule.
The ex-type was resolved with ITS, LSU, beta-tubulin, RPB2, TEF-1-alpha, calmodulin, and actin sequences and placed in a different clade from the Kentucky isolates labeled S. cannabis.
Historical ex-type cultures and sequences for S. cannabis, S. cannabina, and S. neocannabina were unavailable, and the actual distribution and reemergence history remained unknown.
Species-level Septoria naming therefore requires lesion-linked morphology, culture, and validated multilocus evidence rather than lesion appearance or a generic Septoria PCR result alone.

The article figure combines natural lesions, an inoculated leaf, conidiomata, conidia, and culture panels; conflicting license statements and the mixed-panel design prevent admission as training media in this dataset.

sources.title: Leaf Spot Disease Development and Its Effect on Yield of Essential Oil-Producing Hemp Cultivars in Kentucky
supportedClaims: Two Kentucky field experiments in 2020 and 2021 evaluated Bipolaris, Cercospora, and Septoria leaf spots across four essential-oil hemp cultivar groups.
In those experiments Bipolaris was first observed seven to eight weeks after planting and increased through the end of the season; this is a study observation, not a universal onset rule.
All three evaluated leaf spots were more severe in the middle canopy than the upper canopy, and susceptibility differed among cultivar groups; neither pattern is a universal diagnostic threshold.
Reported yield associations concerned the combined leaf-spot disease complex under the tested cultivars, sites, and seasons and must not be attributed to Bipolaris alone.
Overlapping leaf-spot syndromes mean paired canopy observations, temporal follow-up, fungal morphology, culture, and molecular diagnostics are more reliable than one lesion photograph.

sources.title: Septoria Leaf Spot of Hemp
sources.organization: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
sources.publisher: Cornell University Plant Disease Diagnostic Clinic
supportedClaims: The Cornell diagnostic guide describes irregular brown lesions with yellow halos on the upper leaf surface, first appearing on lower leaves and in the inner canopy; coalescing halos can accompany severe defoliation.
Mature lesions can contain small black pycnidia visible to the unaided eye or with a hand lens, and humid lesions may exude thin white curled or ribbon-like conidial tendrils.

Cornell explicitly states that the disease cycle of hemp Septoria species is unknown; debris survival, stomatal infection, moist-season secondary spread, and wind or water dispersal are presented as likely or general Septoria biology rather than fully demonstrated hemp-specific steps.

The guide reports inconsistent field suppression among products and emphasizes airflow, humidity reduction, infected-leaf and debris management, and resistant germplasm research; pesticide use remains subject to current local labels and regulation.
The PDF contains no item-level reusable license for its photographs, so its figures are citation evidence only and are not copied or indexed as dataset media.

sources.title: Efficacy of Organic Fungicides for Management of Hemp Septoria Leaf Spot
supportedClaims: Replicated New York field trials in 2023 and 2024 inoculated the susceptible hemp cultivar TJ's CBD with a single-spore S. cannabis isolate and recorded five severity ratings to calculate area under the disease progress curve.
Azoxystrobin reduced disease progress relative to untreated inoculated controls in both trial years, while other evaluated products were variable or ineffective under the study conditions.

The trial establishes that repeated plant-linked severity measurements can quantify Septoria disease progress; it does not make one cultivar, isolate, location, season, product response, or legal label universal.

Treatment response cannot retroactively confirm an image-only diagnosis, and product selection requires current jurisdiction-specific registration, label compliance, resistance management, and professional guidance.
